Conclusion
Due to the increased bit density of ﬂash memory, the hybrid
SSD technology is becoming more and more important to
enhance write performance. In this paper, we proposed an
RL-based SLC cache technique for the hybrid SSDs. The
proposed method dynamically determines the optimal SLC
cache parameters based on the system states, including the
characteristics of the workload and the internal status of the
SSD. As a result, the write performance is signiﬁcantly en-
hanced without any prior knowledge about host workload or
storage characteristics.
As a future work, we have a plan to examine the effect of
the proposed RL scheme at a real SSD subsystem. Another
work is to apply the technique at multi-stream SSDs [9]. The
host can deliver data separation decisions to a multi-stream
SSD via the stream interface. Different streams tend to have
different update patterns. Thus, we can utilize the stream
information to determine the optimal number of SLC blocks
of each stream by observing the data lifetime of the stream.

第六章.结论
为协同运行的工作负载分配固态硬盘通道是一项关键但
具有挑战性的任务，这既需要遍历庞大的搜索空间，又缺
乏对所谓“最优分配”的统一定义。为此，我们提出了一
种强化学习方法，并开发了名为AutoAlloc的自主通道分配
固态硬盘系统。该系统的导航过程具有三大特点：(i)在运
行时执行；（ii）完全自动化运行；（iii）基于预设的优化
指标。通过多种通道分配场景的测试表明，AutoAlloc仅需
学习少量候选方案，即可找到接近最优的分配方案。

we present the background needed to understand our scheme.
We describe in detail the design and implementation of our
scheme in Section III, and then present our experimental results
on a real hardware platform in Section IV. The related work is

II. BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION
In this section, we classify the NAND flash memories and
identify the advantages and disadvantages of each type of
memory technology. Then, we study the journaling mechanism
of EXT4 file system to understand our scheme in detail. Fi-
nally, we briefly describe our motivation.
A. Classification of NAND flash memories
In general, NAND based flash memories can be classified
into three program modes: SLC, MLC, and TLC. The mode of
flash memory is determined by the number of bits that can be
stored in a single cell. As is well-known, a denser the program
mode provides a higher capacity in the flash memory at the
same manufacturing costs. Unfortunately, a denser program
mode is considered to have a negative impact in that it signif-
icantly reduces the performance and endurance of the flash
memory.
To remedy the disadvantages of using TLC, some manu-
facturers have started to commercialize hybrid flash storage
composed of SLC and TLC program modes [14], [15]. The
storage employs flash memory in the SLC mode as a buffer for
the TLC to temporarily handle incoming data as fast as possi-
ble. Then, all of the data in the SLC buffer is simultaneously
migrated to the flash memory of the TLC program mode during
idle time. However, this type of storage operates at the per-
formance levels of TLC if there is no free space in the SLC
buffer.
To clearly understand the performance gap in real world
systems, we measured the write throughput on the commercial
SSD consisting of hybrid flash storage. In this test, we em-
ployed FIO microbenchmark [16] to continuously issue write
operations

VII. RELATED WORKS
Many prior studies have discussed the design of hybrid
SSD that contains two types of ﬂash chips for the purpose of
improving lifetime and performance. S. Lee et al.[5] proposed
FlexFS that divides storage space of SSD to an SLC zone
and an MLC zone, where user writes are forwarded to SLC
zone, and then data in the SLC zone are migrated to TLC
zone. To mitigate the negative impact of data migration in
FlexFS, they developed a background migration technique that
triggers data migration during idle time, a dynamic allocation
technique that forwards user writes to MLC directly, and a
locality-aware data management technique that retains hot data
in the SLC zone and migrates cold data to the TLC zone.
L. Chang[6] also considered the design of SLC-MLC hybrid
SSD, and proposed the idea of writing hot data to the SLC
zone while writing cold data directly to the TLC zone, which
reduces the amount of data migrated from the SLC zone
to the TLC zone. Similarly, S. Im and D. Shin[7] proposed
ComboFTL that also focus on the management of hot/cold
data in SLC-MLC hybrid SSD, where data can not only be
moved from the SLC zone to the MLC zone but also the
other way around. Speciﬁcally, cold data in the SLC zone
are migrated to the MLC zone, while hot data are migrated
in the opposite direction. Cognizant of the fact that SLC ﬂash
chips are worn out faster than MLC/TLC ﬂash chips in hybrid
SSD because the former absorb the vast majority of writes,

In scenarios where 4 co-runner workloads are executed on a
32-channel, 128GB SSD (and thus, there exist 969 different

Overall, this paper makes the following major contributions:
• We propose an autonomic channel allocating SSD, called
AutoAlloc, which employs an RL-centric approach to ex-
plore channel allocations for a given set of co-running work-
loads. AutoAlloc can reach a near-optimal allocation auto-
matically and gradually at runtime.
• We introduce various desirable definitions of the optimality
and employ them in AutoAlloc. Our experiments reveal
that, for a fixed set of co-running workloads, AutoAlloc
navigates over different candidates and selects different near-
optimal allocations under different definitions.
• We observe that the search space of the allocation problem
can be extremely large, where AutoAlloc becomes a more
effective alternative. In particular, increasing the allocation
granularity can reduce the number of evaluated allocations sig-
nificantly while still coming up with a near-optimal allocation.

the co-running workloads (since a channel is the largest unit
for accessing the storage media). Fig. 1b illustrates an example

The evaluation of our online learning-based classification system was conducted using a rigorous and comprehensive
approach to ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of our algorithm. The dataset utilized in our evaluation was collected
in real-world workloads using the Drmemtrace tool, a powerful utility designed for tracing and analyzing memory
access patterns in various applications.
Data Collection and Preparation. We instrumented the Drmemtrace tool to attach a statistical module to the target
processes, sampling memory access instructions at a rate of 10%. This approach allowed us to capture a representative
subset of the memory access behavior without incurring excessive overhead. The applications selected for data
collection spanned four diverse domains: artificial intelligence computations, big data processing, graph computations,

Finally, we evaluated the effect of MLC region unit size ex-
plained at Section 5. Fig. 16 shows MLC region garbage collection
costs of ComboFTL while varying the unit size. Since the MLC re-
gion has only cold data, a large unit is proﬁtable to increase the uti-

the unit size, more memory space is required for address mapping
since page-level mapping is used within a unit. Therefore, we
should consider both GC cost and space overhead to determine
the unit size.
7. Conclusion
SLC/MLC combined architecture can increase both I/O perfor-
mance and lifespan of ﬂash memory compared to the use of
MLC-only ﬂash memory. To maximize the advantage of such a hy-
brid architecture, it is important to efﬁciently exploit the SLC re-
gion of SLC/MLC combined ﬂash memory. ComboFTL utilizes the
SLC region for frequently updated data using a hot/cold data detec-
tion algorithm and the N-chance algorithm for cold data migration.
It can adjust several policies to handle dynamic workload changes
at run time. In future work, we will study how to determine the
optimal size of the SLC region since it affects performance, lifespan,
and storage capacity of SLC/MLC combined memory.

HAML-SSD: A Hardware Accelerated
Hotness-Aware Machine Learning based SSD
Management
Bingzhe Li∗, Chunhua Deng†, Jinfeng Yang‡, David Lilja‡, Bo Yuan†, and David Du∗
∗Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota

{lixx1743, yang3116, lilja, du}@umn.edu, chunhua.deng@rutgers.edu, bo.yuan@soe.rutgers.edu
Abstract—Solid state drive (SSD) as a fast storage device
has been playing an important role across many applications
from mobile computing to large distributed systems in recent
years. However, the performance of the SSD can be degraded
tremendously due to the intrinsic properties of NAND-based ﬂash
memory including limited erase cycles and asymmetric write and
erase operations. Previous works separated hot/cold data into
different blocks in order to improve SSD performance. ”Hotness”
is typically deﬁned as the cumulative update frequencies of pages.
However, we believe that an additional new parameter, average
update time interval, should also be considered into the ”hotness”
deﬁnition associated with the update frequency. Moreover, to
adaptively classify hot/cold data, a machine learning algorithm
is applied to better accommodate the dynamically changed I/O
access patterns of traces. In this paper, a machine learning (ML)
based SSD management called HAML-SSD is proposed. The
purpose of applying the ML algorithm is to dynamically cluster
the data with similar ”hotness” based on a new deﬁnition of
”hotness”. Thus, a two-dimension clustering algorithm is used
for storing the pages categorized into the same cluster within
the same block. Moreover, to obtain reasonable training time,
a speciﬁc hardware component called HAML-unit is designed
in the SSD. Finally, the experimental results indicate that the
HAML-SSD decreases the response time around 26.3% - 57.7%
compared to previous works with the eval

Both ﬂash memory and NVRAM are written in a log-
structured fashion. Remap-SSD-LH logically divides ﬂash
superblocks into a data superblock pool and an RMM
superblock pool. We refer to the number of RMM superblocks
as R, while the rest are data superblocks. An upper limit is
set for R, say Rmax. A ﬂash superblock is dynamically allo-
cated to store RMM or host data on demand (wear leveling
can be conducted across all ﬂash superblocks), while the num-
ber limit in each pool is guaranteed. When free space in one
superblock pool or NVRAM is running out, GC is performed
in data/RMM superblocks or NVRAM segments to reclaim
invalid data. Both superblock pools reserve at least one free
superblock for migrating valid data during GC.
Assume the sizes of an RMM entry, a superblock, and
NVRAM are Sentry, Ssb, and Snvram, respectively, and there
are Nrp unique logical pages that have been remapped (i.e.,
the size of valid RMM is Nrp ∗Sentry). If NVRAM is large
enough for RMM storage (Snvram >= Nrp ∗Sentry), Rmax is
equal to zero. Otherwise

necessary GC operations under both enterprise and consumer workloads, thereby

5. Conclusion
In this paper, we propose CSTWS, a cost-aware self-tuning write strategy to im-
prove the overall performance of homogeneous hybrid SSDs. First, the WCM mod-
ule models the write costs of the SLC and TLC modes by jointly considering GC
overhead and wear leveling cost, and uses the resulting model to adaptively regulate
the proportion of write requests allocated to the SLC mode. In addition, the WAD
module assigns each write request to a more suitable mode according to data hotness
and channel busyness, thereby alleviating write amplification and reducing write
latency. Finally, the MGC module migrates valid pages from reclaimed SLC blocks
to TLC blocks during GC in the SLC mode, thereby reserving more SLC blocks
for hot write data. Extensive experiments on six enterprise and consumer work-
loads show that, compared with the baseline and representative schemes, CSTWS
significantly reduces average response time and write amplification.

A. Experimental Setups
1) Settings: We implement AGC in an open-source multi-
queue SSD simulator named MQSim [15]. MQSim accurately
simulates the front- and back-end components of modern multi-
queue SSDs. The simulation parameters are listed in Table III.
The approach to selecting blocks in GC is RGA. Its default hot-
cold data separation method deﬁnes the user data as hot while
the valid page data as cold. Initially, we utilize a preconditioning
function in MQSim to initialize the SSD space before loading
the trace, which ensures that GC is triggered under traces.
Similar to work [6], the preconditioning ratio is set to 80%.
We set the buffer size to 1 MB, accommodating 128 valid
pages for GC. The time window size is conﬁgured as 5 ms.
The parallel resource conﬁgurations in Table III include 2-4-

numbers represent the number of channels, chips per channel,
dies per chip, and planes per die, respectively. These conﬁg-
urations are widely adopted in SSD architectures in the past
studies. Through these parallelism conﬁgurations, we are posi-
tioned to investigate the performance of AGC with various SSD
organizations.
2) Alternative Schemes: We compare AGC with four state-
of-the-art schemes which are implem

the freshness and retention time of the data stored in these
pages may vary signiﬁcantly.
Different from these works, this paper exploits the spe-
ciﬁc retention time requirement of data to-be-stored in ﬂash
memory. Retention time is predicted based on the demand-
ing requirement. With this approach, refresh operation is
minimized, and the wearing caused by P/E cycling can be
reduced.
2) Reduce Write Errors: Write errors are originated from
program and erase operations. Program operations inject
charges to the FG, and erase operations remove the charges.
Both program and erase operations induce damages to
the ﬂash memory cells. The damages accumulate over the
P/E cycles.
The design of the P/E operations is very important to the
wearing of ﬂash memory. Jeong et al. [17], [18] showed that
P/E operations with lower threshold voltages induce less ﬂash
wearing. However, lower threshold voltages would result in
smaller noise margins between the various states of cells, and
in turn leads to higher error rates. Based on the observa-
tion, they proposed to slow down the program speed because
slower program speeds cause smaller error rates. Obviously,
their approach would impact write performance especially for
the write intensive applications.
The proposed approach also uses lower threshold voltages
to reduce wearing. Unlike the works in [17] and [18], the
proposed approach exploits the speciﬁc retention time require-
ments of data to-be-stored in the ﬂash memory. Since retention
time required by most of data is much less than the worst case,

We believe that our optimal cleaning strategy is relatively inde-
pendent of the mechanism used to track hot and cold pages; Park
and Du’s Bloom ﬁlter-based recency estimator is likely to be a good
substitute for our resource-intensive algorithm, and other tracking
mechanisms may work as well. Finally, and most signiﬁcantly, un-
like prior work, our work provides models for predicting the effect
of spatial locality on performance, and for parameterizing an FTL
to achieve optimal performance in the presence of locality.
8.
Conclusions
In this work we have presented an exact, close-form model for
block cleaning performance of the greedy collection algorithm under
uniformly distributed trafﬁc, and of LRU cleaning with a simple
hot/cold data mix as well as more complex workloads; in addition
we provide a highly accurate approximation for greedy cleaning with
hot and cold data. We validate the prediations of these models in
simulation, on both synthetic data and (in the case of LRU cleaning)
real workloads. In addition we use these models to derive new insight
into the behavior of cleaning algorithms when data is segregated by
update frequency (“hot/cold data separation”), providing a control
algorithm which is optimal for simple trafﬁc mixes and demonstrates
high performance for real-world workloads. We believe this work
represents a new approach to the issue of Flash Translation Layer
performance, based on a fundamental understanding of how actual
and achievable performance is determined by workload statistics.

为进一步验证WHGC 中各关键机制的有效性与独立贡献, 本文设计了两组消融实验, 分别评估写入模式感知
阈值机制与热度分级迁移机制对系统性能的影响. 通过在保留其余模块不变的前提下, 逐一屏蔽上述关键机制, 并
与完整WHGC 方法进行对比, 可揭示各模块在控制GC 触发频率、降低写放大系数与有效页迁移开销等方面的
具体作用, 从而验证其设计的合理性与必要性. 本组实验基于SSDsim 平台进行, 实验配置与表1 一致. 完整WHGC
方法采用与主实验相同的参数设置. 所使用的数据集为prxy_0 负载, 该数据具有高写入比例与频繁更新特征, 能
够显著呈现不同机制对系统性能的影响.

For SSDs with large capacity and limited DRAM space, DFTL stores the entire mapping table on ﬂash chips and only keep some active mapping entries in a CMT residing in DRAM. Most of the existing FTL schemes [9], [10] gen- erally adopt or extend the architecture of DFTL [8] shown in Fig. 3(a). DFTL uses the segmented LRU [12] to manage the CMT. When the cache is full, it will evict a mapping entry from cache. DFTL packs evicted mapping entries into transla- tion pages in the order of their LPNs. All the mapping entries in the same translation page are logically consecutive. The translation pages on ﬂash chips are tracked with a GTD. If an evicted entry has been updated, all mapping entries in the translation page it resides in should be read, updated, and then rewritten to a free physical page. III. THE PROPOSED APRAD
A. OVERALL ARCHITECTURE
Fig. 1 shows the overall architecture of APRAD for homo-
geneous hybrid SSDs, where TLC flash blocks are logically
partitioned into SLC mode and TLC mode regions. APRAD
models the write cost of different partition configurations
based on hard disk utilization and hot data rate, and analyti-
cally derives the cost-optimal SLC/TLC partition ratio, which
are realized by the WCM and ORD modules. At runtime, the
partition ratio is dynamically adjusted by reconfiguring flash
block modes through the PRA module, enabling adaptive
write optimization under varying workloads.
B. WRITE COST MODELING MODULE
The WCM module models write cost under different
SLC/TLC partition configurations to support quantitative par-
tition management in homogeneous hybrid SSDs. Unlike
prior designs such as TLC-FTL and HFTL, which rely on
qualitative heuristics or empirical tuning, WCM incorporates
flash utilization and hot data rate to capture mode-specific

In this paper, we propose a workload-aware ﬂash translation
layer, named Balloon-FTL , for TLC/SLC dual-mode ﬂash memory
in embedded systems, to improve performance and lifespan of the
system. Balloon-FTL consists of two modules: a workload identiﬁer
and a hybrid mapping mechanism. Workload identiﬁer is proposed
to dynamically determine the TLC/SLC capacity based on workload
of different applications. We design two workload-aware strategies
for different situations, including a mathematic formulation for low
latency environment, and a genetic algorithm for long using time
environment. Hybrid mapping mechanism is proposed for mapping
pages at distinct granularity in TLC/SLC dual-mode ﬂash memory
according to different I/O workloads. To achieve this, a page-level
mapping is adopted to handle random and hot sequential requests,
while a block-level mapping is adopted to handle cold sequential
requests. Evaluation results show that Balloon-FTL can effectively
improve the system performance and lifespan.

热度分级的垃圾回收方法WHGC (write pattern-aware and heat-
tiered garbage collection), 以实现GC 性能与设备寿命的协同优化. 该方法的核心机制包括: 基于主机写入行为动态
感知系统负载, 自适应调整GC 触发阈值, 实现灵活的GC 调度策略; 结合空间利用率与块擦除状态构建评分模型,
以指导回收块选择; 构建逻辑页热度等级与块擦除等级的映射机制, 实现热度感知的数据迁移与磨损均衡调控.
综上, 本文的主要贡献如下.
(1) 提出一种写入模式感知的GC 触发机制, 结合主机写入行为动态调整触发阈值, 提升系统对负载状态变化
的自适应能力.
(2) 提出一种基于逻辑页热度等级与块擦除等级的映射迁移机制, 实现逻辑页活跃度与物理块磨损状态之间
的协调匹配, 提升数据迁移的合理性.
(3) 在多个典型工作负载下, 对所提方法与主流GC 策略进行对比评估, 实验结果验证了WHGC 在写放大控
制、有效页迁移开销与延长设备使用寿命能力等方面具有综合优势.
本文第1 节介绍垃圾回收的研究背景与相关工作. 第2 节介绍WHGC 方法的设计原理与实现机制. 第3 节通
过对比实验验证本文所提方法的有效性. 第4 节总结全文.

3.3 本章小结
本章首先介绍了2 种经典的异质混合固态硬盘闪存转换层算法——CFTL 和ComboFTL。
在此基础上，分析了CFTL 和ComboFTL 的不足，提出了一种按需加载的基于SLC 和MLC
闪存的异质混合SSD 的FTL 算法，简称HDFTL。HDFTL 解决了混合SSD 的统一地址映射
问题，SLC / MLC 数据分配问题，以及SLC 和MLC 区域之间的损耗均衡的问题。首先，
HDFTL 以4KB 大小对齐SLC 和MLC 的数据页，统一采用按需加载的地址映射机制。 所有
的翻译页都存储在SLC 区中，然后根据需要加载到缓存映射表中。其次，HDFTL 利用数据
更新和地址映射项更新的一致性，结合缓存映射表设计，提出了一种基于HW-CMT 命中的热
写数据识别方案，以解决写数据分配问题。最后，HDFTL 利用SLC 和MLC 闪存区的相对磨
损速率来动态调整HW-CMT 的大小，进而改变热写数据识别基准和数据分配的结果，使得
SLC 和MLC 闪存之间的相对磨损均衡效果更好。实验结果表明，与CFTL 和ComboFTL 相
比，HDFTL 所需的CMT 存储开销最少，性能最佳。

ABSTRACT
Efficient management of storage resources in big data and cloud computing environments requires
accurate identification of data’s "cold" and "hot" states. Traditional methods, such as rule-based
algorithms and early AI techniques, often struggle with dynamic workloads, leading to low accuracy,
poor adaptability, and high operational overhead. To address these issues, we propose a novel
solution based on online learning strategies. Our approach dynamically adapts to changing data
access patterns, achieving higher accuracy and lower operational costs. Rigorous testing with both
synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates a significant improvement, achieving a 90% accuracy
rate in hot-cold classification. Additionally, the computational and storage overheads are considerably
reduced.
1
Introduction
In the contemporary landscape of big data and cloud computing, the efficient management of storage resources has
emerged as a paramount concern. One of the most critical aspects of this challenge is the accurate identification of
data’s "cold" and "hot" states. Data is classified as "hot" if it is frequently accessed, necessitating fast and readily
available storage solutions. Conversely, "cold" data, which is rarely accessed, can be stored more cost-effectively in
slower, less expensive storage mediums. Effective hot-cold identification not only optimizes storage costs but also
enhances system performance by ensuring that the most relevant data is quickly accessible[1, 2, 3].
The importance of hot-cold data identification cannot be overstated. In large-scale data centers, the ability to distinguish
between hot and cold data can lead to substantial savings in both storage and energy costs[4]. Moreover, it plays a
crucial role in improving the overall efficiency of dat

Hybrid approaches combine multiple rule-based policies to improve accuracy and adaptability. For example, the

fixed rules and may not adapt well to highly dynamic environments.

V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we propose a workload-aware ﬂash transla-
tion layer, named TLC-FTL, for TLC/SLC dual-mode ﬂash
memory in embedded systems. TLC-FTL gets a balanced
trade-off in performance and lifetime between the TLC mode
and SLC mode by mapping pages at different granularities
according to different I/O workloads. It consists a hybrid
mapping strategy and a workload aware strategy. The hybrid
mapping strategy adopts page-level mapping to handle random
and hot sequential requests, while block-level mapping for
most cold sequential requests.W The workload aware strategy
is proposed to dynamically determine the number of SLC
blocks based on different applications. We have conducted
a series of experiments with realistic I/O traces. Evaluation
results show that TLC-FTL can effectively improve the system
performance and lifetime.

B. EVALUATION METHODOLOGIES
To evaluate ML-based SSD optimization techniques, re-
searchers have adopted three primary methodologies: simu-
lation, trace-based analysis, and prototype implementation.
Each approach provides a different balance between realism,
control, scalability, and engineering complexity, and their
adoption often reflects the nature of the ML technique or
target optimization.
Simulation-based evaluation is widely used in early-stage
studies where low-cost experimentation and internal observ-
ability are essential. SSD simulators [73], [74], [96]–[98] pro-
vide researchers with fine-grained control over internal mech-
anisms such as the FTL, GC, and caching. For example, Sun
et al. [43] employed SSDSim [97] to evaluate a supervised
caching classifier, while Zhang et al. [46] used FlashSim [98]
to test an RL-based cache management strategy. Simulation
is particularly effective for controlled comparisons of algo-
rithmic policies under synthetic workloads, although it may
abstract away timing inaccuracies, wear leveling behavior, or
hardware-induced variability found in real devices.
Trace-based experiments are preferred when testing ML
models that depend heavily on real-world access patterns,
such as those used in prefetching or hot/cold data classifica-
tion. By replaying I/O traces collected from actual production
environments, researchers can evaluate how models gener-
alize to realistic, complex workloads. For instance, Deep-
Prefetcher [49] and ML-DT [60] used cloud-server traces
to evaluate neural network-based sequence prediction and
data lifespan modeling. While trace-driven evaluation offers
realism, it may not reflect closed-loop interactions between
ML models and SSD internals.
Prototype implementations provide the most realistic in-
sights by validating ML models on actual SSD hardware
or FPGA platforms. This method is commonly used in re-
search involving in-storage processing or hardware-aware
optimizations. For example,

such that it does not require a large memory space. Therefore, pure
page-level mapping is also unsuitable. Considering these two con-
ﬂicting requirements, ComboFTL adopted the unit-based page-le-
vel mapping [20], instead of the block-level mapping for the MLC
region used in our previous work [19].
In the unit-based page-level mapping, one unit consists of mul-
tiple sequential logical blocks similar to the superblock FTL [5], and
several physical blocks can be allocated to the unit. There is a limit
on the number of physical blocks that can be allocated to a unit.
Each page can be written at any physical page within the physical
blocks allocated to the corresponding unit. Therefore, page-level
mapping information within only the unit boundary is required
and the size of mapping information is smaller than that of pure

IV. EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES
A. Experimental Settings
This section investigates the performance of the proposed
utilization-aware self-tuning design (referred to as UST)
through a trace-driven simulation. In order to demonstrate
the advantages of the variable-sized SLC buffer of UST,
we implemented two well-known efﬁcient ﬁxed-sized SLC
buffer FTL designs, namely, HFTL and SW-CTRL (revised
from [4] and [13], respectively), for comparison. Both HFTL
and SW-CTRL allocate a small ﬁxed number of SLC blocks to
work as a ﬁxed-sized SLC buffer and manage the SLC buffer
through a page-level mapping strategy, so as to efﬁciently
handle write requests; meanwhile, when the buffer is full
(of valid data and/or invalid data), both designs will evict the
seldom-updated data from the SLC buffer into TLC block area,
which is managed through a block-level mapping strategy,
to accommodate more write requests. In addition, we also

Some prior work [22]-[27] focused on using hybrid SLC/
MLC ﬂash memory to improve SSD write performance. Write
requests are ﬁrst stored in SLC region at a higher speed and
then migrated to MLC region later on if necessary. Prior work
proposed different region partition and data migration strat-

Pan et al. [6] proposed to dynamically adjust ﬂash pro-
gramming speed according to the run-time P/E cycling num-

always close to what can be maximally tolerated by the
existing redundancy. Our approach also aims to dynamically
adjust ﬂash memory programming speed. However, we
change the programming speed according to the workload
dynamic characteristic instead of run-time P/E cycling

CONCLUSION
This paper presents a design approach to improve the SSD
write performance by exploiting run-time data access work-
load variation and temporal locality at the system level and
NAND ﬂash memory write latency vs. data retention time
trade-off at the device level. The basic idea is to perform
unconventional fast write at the penalty of data retention time
when the run-time workload is intensive and rewrite those
fast-written pages when the SSD is idle. We develop various
techniques to facilitate the practical implementation of this
design concept to reduce the impact on cycling endurance.
The effects of various design parameters in this design ap-
proach are also discussed. The simulation and analysis results
based on detailed ﬂash memory cell models and SSD system
simulator suggest that up to 52.3% SSD average response time
reduction can be achieved.

A. COMPARISON BY RESEARCH TOPIC
Research on ML-driven SSD optimization can be categorized
into four major areas: I/O performance optimization, data
management and optimization, reliability and endurance, and
advanced SSD architectures. Below, we summarize key stud-

1) I/O Performance Optimization with Internal DRAM
The goal of caching, write buffer management, and prefetch-
ing in SSDs is to reduce I/O latency, avoid unnecessary writes,
and maximize resource efficiency. Traditional heuristics, such
as LRU or sequential detectors, are often inadequate under
irregular or dynamic workloads. ML techniques offer the
ability to learn access patterns, classify request types, and
make proactive decisions that static methods cannot.

I/O requests based on temporal and statistical features. This
enables systems to retain high-impact data in the cache or
avoid buffering low-reuse writes, thereby reducing WA and
improving performance. RL [46] offers another dimension of
adaptability, allowing systems to optimize cache replacement

2.2. Motivation
Write latency differs significantly between the LSB and MSB pages of TLC flash
memory. Using only the LSB pages can therefore substantially reduce write la-
tency. However, this also reduces storage capacity, increases GC frequency, and
may eventually degrade flash performance. A subset of TLC flash blocks can thus
be configured in the SLC mode, while the remaining blocks operate in the TLC
mode. By properly balancing the ratio of the two modes, TLC flash can improve
write performance without excessive capacity loss. To fully exploit the complemen-
tary advantages of the two modes, three key issues must be addressed: how to
regulate write-request allocation between the SLC and TLC modes, how to select
the appropriate mode for each write request, and how to design a GC mechanism
coordinated with the two modes.
Due to differences in flash workload characteristics, the write costs of the SLC
mode and the TLC mode change over time. If the system directs more requests
to SLC blocks, although these blocks can process requests faster, the increasing
number of writes reduces SLC free space and raises its write cost. Under such
conditions, continuing to assign many requests to the SLC mode may not improve

smaller memory cell operational noise margin will directly

fundamental trade-off between NAND ﬂash memory pro-
gramming speed and data retention time. This makes it
possible to temporally boost memory programming speed
at the cost of data retention time, which has already been used
in latest commercial products [3]. The above discussion sug-

Whenever necessary, we temporally boost NAND ﬂash mem-

time. Since those fast-written data have very short data
retention time (e.g., few weeks or days instead of several
months or years), we should rewrite those data in time to

3.4. Mode-Aware Garbage Collection Module
To ensure efficient space reclamation in the SLC/TLC dual-mode organization,
CSTWS incorporates a mode-aware garbage collection (MGC) module. MGC co-
ordinates reclamation by jointly considering the flash operating mode and the free-
page status at runtime. Although TLC-FTL 13 allocates hot data to the SLC mode,
it does not coordinate GC across the two modes. In contrast, CSTWS couples recla-
mation in the SLC and TLC modes, allowing valid-page migration and free-space
recovery to be coordinated when necessary. This coordinated design helps improve
space utilization and maintain stable performance under dynamic workloads.
CSTWS continuously monitors the free-page ratios of the two modes, denoted by
fSLC and fTLC. When either ratio falls below the GC threshold thg, the GC process
gets triggered. Specifically, a low free-page ratio in the SLC mode triggers SLC-GC,
while a low free-page ratio in the TLC mode triggers TLC-GC. SLC-GC and TLC-
GC work together to reclaim space in both SLC and TLC blocks efficiently. Once
SLC-GC gets triggered, valid pages in the chosen SLC block are migrated to TLC
blocks. Migration within the same mode gets minimized by this approach, and SLC
space gets preserved for subsequent requests assigned to the SLC mode. If enough
space in the TLC blocks cannot be found, TLC-GC gets triggered proactively by
CSTWS to make sure valid-page migration succeeds. Once TLC-GC gets triggered,
TLC blocks are reclaimed to provide free pages in the TLC mode. Through the
integration of these mode-aware GC mechanisms, CSTWS reduces write amplifica-
tion, mitigates performance degradation, and maintains stable performance across
workloads. The GC results are fed back to guide subsequent threshold adjustments,
ensuring balanced space utilization and sustained performance.

VI. CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES
This survey has examined recent advances in applying ML to
SSD optimization, spanning key areas such as performance
enhancement, data placement, endurance improvement, and
architectural innovation. We systematically categorized over
40 representative studies and conducted comparative analyses
across research themes, learning methodologies, evaluation
approaches, and overhead mitigation techniques. Our find-
ings indicate that ML is emerging as a transformative enabler
for addressing long-standing challenges in SSDs, including
GC inefficiency, write amplification, and reliability degrada-
tion.
A notable trend is the increasing diversity and maturity
of ML approaches. While early studies relied on lightweight
supervised models, recent work has embraced DL, RL, and
hybrid techniques that offer greater flexibility and adaptabil-
ity. In parallel, there is a growing emphasis on real-time
responsiveness, online learning, and hardware acceleration to
meet the strict performance and resource constraints of SSD
environments. Encouragingly, an increasing number of stud-
ies are now moving beyond simulation, implementing ML-
based controllers on prototype systems and demonstrating
their practical viability.
Despite this progress, several challenges remain unre-
solved. The limited computational capacity and memory
bandwidth of SSD controllers impose strict constraints on
model complexity and inference latency. In addition, existing
ML-based solutions often operate in silos, optimizing individ-
ual subsystems without consideration for global trade-offs.
Furthermore, the scarcity of diverse and realistic workload
datasets continues to limit the generalizability, reproducibil-
ity, and fair benchmarking of proposed techniques.

VI. CONCLUSION
With the rapid development of NAND ﬂash memory tech- niques, ﬂash-based SSDs have been widely used in an enterprise-scale storage system. However, the increasing capac- ity of SSDs requires a large DRAM space to hold the mapping table in a page-level FTL. With the limited built-in DRAM space, this article proposes a novel page-level FTL scheme, HCFTL, which clusters newly evicted mapping entries into DTPs, for speeding up the subsequent accesses. HCFTL addi- tionally employs DTPIs to enable fast queries for determining if a mapping entry is in a DTP. A Ghost-CMT, which is an auxiliary cache, is introduced to improve efﬁciency of the indexes and reduce the negative impacts imposed by bloom ﬁlters. Ghost-CMT can sort evicted mapping entries by their LPNs and produce dynamic pages with minimum difference between the maximal and minimal LPNs of entries in those pages. 的过早或滞后触发; 引入指数衰减型逻辑页热度识别策略, 准确反映数据的写入活跃度, 实现冷热数据的有效区分;
并通过热度等级与擦除等级映射的有效页迁移策略, 实现数据热度与物理块磨损状态的合理匹配, 提升了有效页
迁移效率与空间利用率. 实验结果表明, 相较于对比方法, WHGC 的主机写入量平均至少提升了18.88%, 并在写放
大系数、GC 触发频率、擦除次数标准差等多个关键指标上均表现出较优性能, 验证了所提方法的有效性与实用
价值. 未来工作将尝试引入机器学习技术进一步提升数据热度识别的准确性, 并探索该方法与文件系统层的协同
机制, 通过融合数据语义与生命周期信息, 优化GC 决策流程, 进一步增强SSD 的可靠性与智能化管理能力.

5) Comparative Analysis by ML Technique
ML techniques used in SSD optimization vary not only in
structure but also in how they address different challenges
across the storage stack. The choice of technique depends on
the optimization target, whether it involves precise classifi-
cation, long-term adaptation, or complex pattern recognition,
and the type of feedback or data structure available.
Supervised learning has been effective in problems where
workload characteristics can be captured through static fea-
tures. For instance, CCache [43] and NCache [44] used RFs
and Decision Trees to classify I/O requests by criticality
and re-access likelihood, enabling selective cache retention
and eviction. Similarly, Wu et al. [55] applied supervised
models to trigger GC by learning from system states like
page validity ratios and queue depth. These cases show how
supervised learning supports fast and interpretable decisions
where labeled data is available.
Unsupervised learning is most commonly used in data
placement tasks, where distinguishing hot and cold data is
critical but ground truth labels are not available. Lu et al. [59]
and Li et al. [61] used clustering techniques to group data
by lifespan or update frequency, reducing WA through more
intelligent block assignment. These models uncover latent
structure in access patterns without explicit supervision, mak-
ing them suitable for on-device lifetime-aware management.
RL is well-suited to optimization problems where feed-
back is delayed or goal states evolve over time. Kang et al.
[52] applied Q-learning to GC scheduling, optimizing for
tail latency and system throughput. Similarly, RL-cSSD [79]
managed NAND mode transitions in convertible SSDs by
learning when to switch flash types to balance endurance and
performance. These examples demonstrate RL’s strength in

V. RELATED WORK
Over the past decade, with the development of multi-level cell
technology, the price of NAND flash storage has continuously
been decreased, and the market share of the MLC/TLC NAND
storage has continuously been increased. This is because of two
reasons: first, flash technology has significantly been improved
by the manufacturer, and second, there has been much research
to overcome the disadvantages of using MLC/TLC technology,
such as the lower performance and lifetime. In this section, we
present the related works that have been proposed to overcome
the disadvantages of MLC/TLC technology.
Several studies have been performed on FTL and the file
system level to overcome the low performance and low lifetime
of MLC NAND storage [5]-[7]. Im et al. [5] and Murugan et al.
[6] conducted FTL-level research that selectively writes hot data
to the SLC region. Lee et al. [7] proposed a file system for
combined SLC-MLC storage that uses the SLC region as a write
buffer. These techniques focused on data classification based on
hotness and efficiently improved the overall storage performance
by writing frequently-updated data into the SLC region. Recently,
various studies [25]-[27] proposed techniques suitable for TLC
NAND storage to alleviate its lower performance and endurance

The two-level cache design may impact read performance,
because the sectors belonging to the same logical page spread
across the flash pages in both levels of the cache. To mitigate
the performance degradation caused partial page updates, we
propose distributing the updated data across different paral-
lelism units. For example, when a partial-page update occurs
(e.g., last two sectors of data in LPN0 are updated), our
proposal will merge them with the data of other partial-page
writes (e.g., LPN1) or other partial-page updates to generate
full-page data in the data cache. Then, the merged page will be
flushed to the L1 cache slots located at Channel 1 for avoiding
read conflicts, and two new relevant mapping entries are added
to the SMT.
Note that the sectors belonging to the same logical pages
are stored in adjacent positions within the physical page in
the L1 cache. Figure 4 shows the process of reconstructing
an entire page. As read, when accessing the full page (e.g.,
LPN0), our proposal first queries the SMT to obtain the PPN,
Sector Flag and Off, then it knows which sectors are stored
in the L1 cache and locates their offsets in the physical page.
At last, it can reconstruct the full pages of data to maintain
integrity.

workload behaviors and temporal patterns. In SSDs, they
can be utilized for tasks such as forecasting I/O patterns,
predicting potential failures, or managing caching and

It is quite common for a single resource-rich contemporary
solid-state drive (SSD) to accommodate and execute multiple
workloads simultaneously. Such a shared SSD requires its
internal resources to be partitioned and allocated to co-running
workloads for preventing the competing workloads from in-
terfering with one another. While there exist various ways of
allocating the resources in an SSD, channel-based allocation
strategies are desirable from a performance standpoint, as they
can eliminate any potential interference between the workloads,
and thus, offer performance isolation to each workload [8].
Unfortunately, existing channel-based allocation strategies
assume a specific scenario in which the number of co-running
workloads is quite small, and in turn, each workload can obtain
as many channels as it wants. However, such situations may
not occur in some environments (e.g., university, company)
where many users in an organization share a fixed amount of
resources. Instead, in such environments where the collective
demand of workloads exceeds the available channel capacity,
device operators can face a new critical problem: “what is the
optimal channel allocation for a given set of co-running work-
loads?” In this paper, we refer to this problem as the “channel
allocation problem” and present a novel online solution for it.
The channel allocation problem is quite challenging due
to the following reasons. First, there is no accepted, unified
definition of “optimality”. In situations of channel scarcity, an
increase in the channel allocation for a workload necessarily
leads to a decrease in the channel allocation for another work-
load, in which case the former workload experiences improved
performance whereas the latter workload suffers from degraded
performance. Then, what is the desirable standard that can be
employed to favor one allocation over the other? Second, the
performance of each of the co-running workloads under varying

I. INTRODUCTION
Recently, NAND flash memory-based SSDs have been
widely adopted in personal computers, data centers, and cloud
storage systems due to their high performance, large capacity,
and low power consumption. To enhance the capacity of SSDs,
high-bit-density cells, such as triple-level cells (TLC) or quad-
level cells (QLC), are utilized to store more bits per cell.
Additionally, various three-dimensional (3D) architectures of
NAND flash memory, in conjunction with high bit-density
cells (with TLC as the focus in this discussion), have been
launched into the market to overcome the scaling limit of
planar NAND flash arrays [6, 8, 16]. However, there is no
such thing as a free lunch; while 3D TLC SSDs significantly
increase storage density, they come with poorer performance.
Compared to single-level cell (SLC) or multi-level cell (MLC)
based SSDs, 3D TLC SSDs require more time to decode (read)
or encode (write) data.
As an alternative solution, SLC caches are integrated into
commercial 3D TLC SSDs to mitigate this performance issue
[9, 23, 26]. During host writes, data is first written to a limited-
capacity SLC cache, leveraging the higher performance of
SLCs to deliver better overall SSD performance. SLC cache is
cleared during idle time to sustainably provide enough space
for following writes. However, two key challenges arise from
the characteristics of SLC caches: 1) The limited SLC cache
can quickly become saturated under sustained write workloads.
Due to the low bit density of SLC, hybrid 3D SSDs typically
allocate only a small portion of TLC space as an SLC cache,
preserving the capacity advantage of hybrid 3D SSDs. Once
saturated, sustained writes are redirected to the TLC space
and are processed at TLC performance levels, leading to a
performance cliff; 2) The reclamation process for the SLC
cache results in a large amount of additional writes. The SLC

C. Read Performance Optimization
Since read requests need to read the data from the flash
memory, they tend to experience longer end-to-end latency.
Consequently, read performance is more sensitive than write
performance in SSDs. Prior research has focused on opti-
mizing the read performance of SSDs, in two typical cate-
gories: prefetch and data placement. The first category involves
prefetching data based on historical access patterns and char-
acteristics [13], [14]. Previous research has proposed using
intelligent algorithms such as machine learning [13] and deep
reinforcement learning [14] to achieve highly accurate data
prediction. However, these approaches often face the challenge
of computational overhead. In the second category, the main
bottleneck in the read performance of hybrid SSDs lies in
reading data from high-latency pages. To mitigate this issue,
hybrid SSDs store frequently accessed data in pages with low
latency [7], [8]. However, since the number of pages with
low latency is limited, allocating all frequently accessed data
to these pages inevitably limits the opportunity to improve
write performance. Additionally, when the workload pattern
changes, the data allocation process needs to be performed
again, resulting in additional overhead for reallocation.
III. MOTIVATION
The work begins by emphasizing the importance of un-
derstanding the read data distribution in hybrid SSDs before
addressing read performance enhancements. Our preliminary
evaluation tests nine workloads and identifies the TLC area
as the main source of read data, accounting for over 70%
of read requests on average, as shown by Baseline in
Figure 7, potentially creating a bottleneck due to increased
read latency. Section V provides a more detailed evaluation
setup. Additionally, the limited capacities of SLC buffer and
RAM buffer hinder their effectiveness in handling read data.

VI. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we present an efficient scheme to improve the
performance and lifetime of combined SLC-TLC storage.
Specifically, we reserved dedicated space for the journal data
on the high-speed SLC region to employ the I/O characteristics
of the file system journaling. We separated the journal data
from the host writes to reduce the overhead of the garbage
collection and data migration, and we wrote the journal data on
the reserved SLC region to reduce its synchronous journal write
latency. We implemented our scheme on a real storage platform
and conducted a series of experiments with various workloads.
The experimental results show that our scheme significantly
improves the performance and lifetime of the storage.

V. RELATED WORK
With the advancement in hybrid SSDs, numerous optimiza-
tion strategies have been proposed to manage the SLC cache.
We summarize them into two categories:
SLC cache management based on hot/cold data separa-
tion. Chang et al. [49] proposed an SLC cache management
for SLC-MLC hybrid SSDs, which forwards the hot data pages
to the SLC cache while the cold data pages to the MLC
region. They also proposed using the k-means algorithm to
estimate the hotness of data pages, for accurately directing
the placement of hot/cold data pages.
To better distinguish the hot/cold data pages, Yao et al. [50]
presented a cache-assisted hot data identification scheme,
which employs the hits on the cached mapping entries to
identify hot data pages, to efficiently guide the placement
of data pages on the SLC cache and the MLC region. In
addition, Kwon et al. [12] partitioned the SLC cache into
fixed-size regions dedicated to system journal data and normal
user data respectively, aiming to reduce the number of valid
page migrations during GC operations in the SLC cache.
Consequently, the negative impact on normal I/O processing
that is caused by GC operations can be greatly minimized.
Dynamically adjusting the size of the SLC cache. Modern
SSDs are designed to support flash cells operating in both
high-density modes (e.g., QLC and TLC) and low-density
modes (e.g., SLC). In such a design, the flash cells in low-
density modes can be utilized as the cache space to improve
the overall performance. Shi et al. [13] proposed a SLC cache
management scheme called HyFlex. It allocates the SLC/QLC
data pages based on request size when running intensive I/O
workloads. The scheme also supports converting the QLC
mode cells to work with the SLC mode, for the purpose of
avoiding frequent GC operations in the SLC cache.

sity increases, traditional rule-based methods face growing
limitations. To address these challenges, researchers have
applied supervised learning, unsupervised learning, RL, and

A. I/O PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION WITH INTERNAL
DRAM
Internal DRAM plays a vital role in bridging the perfor-
mance gap between main memory and NAND flash storage.
It supports efficient caching, write buffering, and prefetching,
which are essential for reducing access latency and improv-
ing endurance. However, traditional management approaches
[25] often perform poorly under dynamic and irregular work-
loads. ML provides a promising alternative by learning access
patterns and adaptively tuning memory behavior. This subsec-
tion reviews how ML enhances caching, write buffering, and
prefetching mechanisms in SSDs.
1) Caching and Write Buffer Management
Efficient cache and write buffer management is critical for
minimizing latency, reducing WA, and extending SSD lifes-
pan. Legacy techniques [5], [10], [11], based on Least Re-
cently Used (LRU), often degrade under unpredictable access
patterns. To address this, ML-based approaches have been
proposed that utilize predictive models to classify I/O re-
quests, assign cache priorities, and dynamically adjust buffer
space allocation.
Sun et al. [43] introduced a cache management scheme
named CCache, which uses a random forest (RF) classifier
to categorize I/O requests into critical, intermediate, and non-
critical classes. Critical requests are preferentially retained

Similar to traditional NAND ﬂash memory, triple-level cell (TLC) ﬂash memory is used as secondary stor-
age to meet the fast growing demands on storage capacity. TLC ﬂash memory exhibits attractive features
such as shock resistance, high density, low cost, non-volatility and low access latency natures. However,
TLC ﬂash memory also has some extra limitations, such as write disturbance, low performances and very
limited cycles compared to single-level cell (SLC) ﬂash memory.
In this paper, we propose a workload-aware ﬂash translation layer, named Balloon-FTL, for the TLC/SLC
dual-mode ﬂash memory, to improve performance and lifespan of the system. We ﬁrst build a work-
load identiﬁer module with genetic algorithm to dynamically allocate TLC/SLC capacity based on differ-
ent workloads, and produce the suitable data allocation to achieve a balanced write distribution in ﬂash
memory with low memory access cost. The

that has been pre-trained at one system is used at other systems,
it can adapt to the new environments in a short time. To check
the effect of the trained agent, we first pre-train an agent with
several other workloads, and then get the performance of the agent
at the six workloads. Figure 8 shows the performance comparison
of the pre-trained and untrained agents (the results are normalized
to the pre-trained agent). The pre-trained agent improves the write
performance by up to 8.65% over the untrained agent. Therefore, we
can know that the RL-based scheme can be applied quickly to a new
system by using a pre-trained agent.
E. Overhead Discussion
The overhead of the proposed scheme mainly includes computation
and memory for running the Q-learning model. In our evaluation,
the Q-learning model is invoked every 1000 I/O requests, but its
influence on the system performance is negligible because it only
consists of a small number of instructions to execute with several
memory accesses. The memory overhead mainly comes from Q-table
size and the entries of Q-table equal to 4 bytes × # of states × # of
actions. As shown in Table IV, when there are eight actions, the
Q-Table is only 14KB. The small Q-table can be easily cached in the
internal DRAM of the SSD.
V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we propose a SLC-MLC-QLC level-based space
management scheme to enhance the performance of convertible
SSDs. A real-time Q-learning model is designed to coordinate when
and how the GC and flash conversion operations should be done
based on the SSD internal status and workload patterns. Experimental
results show that our RL-cSSD scheme effectively improves system
throughput and prevents cliff performance drops with little overhead.

I. INTRODUCTION
Hard drives have been the most widely deployed storage
media for many years. Compared with hard drives, solid state
drives average cost per MB is currently much higher [22].
Although SSDs are still not as popular as hard drives now, they
will certainly be the next preferred storage media because of
the high performance and low power cost compared with those
of HDDs. Two major challenges of SSDs have been addressed
in previous research: random write [5] and reliability. Each
block on ﬂash-based storage media such as SSDs and ﬂash
drives has limited erasure times. Furthermore, each block has
to be erased before it can be rewritten. Erasure operations
reduce both performance and SSDs’ life times of SSDs [4].
People used to believe that access patterns were not cor-
related to SSDs performance, but Chen, Koufaty, and Zhang
indicated that different access patterns may have negative and
positive impacts on internel parallelism [9]. A good FTL
algorithm is able to reduce the impact of access patterns by
balancing workloads at the block level.
Inter-disk parallelism on hard drives has been well studied
for decades. Data Striping, for example, is a typical solution
to enhance inter-disk parallelism. Such parallelism is storage-
media independent, meaning it is effective for hard drive
disks, SSDs, and tapes. Unlike inter-disk parallelism, intra-
disk parallelism is closely related to storage media, therefore,
intra-SSD parallelism needs to be studied despite the fact that
intra-HDD parallelism has already been well explored [28].
Interestingly, because ﬂash-based storage has a unique mech-
anism, parallelism can be applied in multiple levels, namely,
package-level, die-level, and plane-level [10].

Our solution: an online learning-based approach. To address the limitations of traditional methods, we propose a
novel solution based on online learning strategies. Our approach leverages the latest developments in online machine
learning to dynamically adapt to changing data access patterns without the need for extensive pre-training or manual
intervention[20, 21]. By continuously learning from new data, our method can achieve higher accuracy in identifying
cold and hot data, even under highly variable workloads. This dynamic adaptation capability ensures that the model
remains up-to-date and effective, regardless of changes in data access patterns[21]. Moreover, our solution is designed
to be computationally efficient, reducing the operational costs associated with continuous monitoring and manual
adjustments. The reduced need for manual tuning and the ability to scale effectively make our method particularly
suitable for modern data storage systems. Finally, we propose a dynamic hot-cold threshold tuning algorithm for
hot/cold discrimination under different workloads. We have rigorously tested our solution using both synthetic and
real-world datasets. The results demonstrate a significant improvement (up to 90%) in accuracy compared to traditional
methods, while also showing a reduction in computational overhead.

C. Sensitivity Analysis
There are two read retry count threshold parameters in
RARO: R1 and R2. To understand the characteristics of these
two parameters, we conducted a sensitivity study to show
their impact on the overall read performance and capacity
of the device. According to the read retries distribution in
section III, the number of page read retries of the QLC flash
memory in the experiment is centrally located between 4 and
9 in the young stage, between 7 and 12 in the middle stage,
and between 11 and 16 in the old age stage, so the read
retries threshold R2 varies according to the ranges of these
three stages. The TLC flash memory in the experiment is
converted from QLC flash memory, and it is tested under
typical workloads and found that the number of read retries
does not exceed 1, so the read retry threshold R1 is selected
as 1.

conversion from QLC to SLC increases while the conversion

In practice, the thresholds R1 and R2 may need to be adjusted

In this paper, we propose a read optimisation method,

Our research methodology significantly deviates from traditional approaches, as it
does not depend on indirect indicators such as data hotness levels, specific SLC cache sizes,
or predetermined threshold values. This means that the mere classification of data as “hot”
does not automatically justify its storage in the SLC cache. Our approach is more direct and
focused: we aim to precisely evaluate the potential for future reuse of data currently stored
in the SLC cache, moving beyond conventional metrics to a more targeted assessment of
data value for cache management.
To achieve this objective, we employ machine-learning algorithms capable of analyzing
and predicting data reuse patterns. Our approach takes into account the dynamic and
ever-changing nature of workload characteristics, as well as the current operational state of
the SSD. By doing so, we can make more informed and accurate predictions about which
data will be accessed again in the near future. This allows for more efficient use of the SLC
cache, as it ensures that only data with a high probability of reuse occupies this valuable
space, therefore optimizing the overall performance and lifespan of the hybrid SSD.

operating system (OS) levels to enhance caching, I/O schedul-
ing, and file system performance, these approaches generally
treat the SSD as a black box and overlook internal inefficien-
cies [12]–[20]. Internal SSD challenges such as fine-grained
wear leveling, latency variability, and constrained controller
resources necessitate models that are both lightweight and
hardware-aware. Unlike host-side solutions, SSD-internal
ML must operate under strict performance, memory, and
power constraints, making efficient model design and real-
time inference critical.
Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility and ben-
efits of deploying ML directly within SSD firmware. ML-
enabled controllers have been shown to enhance various inter-
nal mechanisms including workload prediction, adaptive GC,
dynamic data placement, and reliability monitoring. In addi-
tion, the evolution of SSD architectures such as multi-stream
SSDs and computational storage devices has introduced new
opportunities for applying intelligent, self-adaptive control
strategies that go beyond static rule-based logic.
While several prior surveys have addressed ML applica-
tions in broader storage or system-level contexts [21]–[24],
few have systematically focused on the unique challenges
and opportunities associated with deploying ML inside SSDs.
This paper aims to bridge that gap by providing a structured
and comprehensive review of SSD-internal ML research,
emphasizing hardware-level constraints and real-time design
considerations.
The contributions of this survey are threefold:
• We provide a taxonomy of ML techniques applied
directly to SSD-internal operations, includ

achines (SVM) [31], decision trees [32], and neural
networks [33]. This approach is widely used in classification
tasks, such as spam detection, image recognition, and work-
load prediction. It is particularly useful in scenarios where
historical data with known outcomes is available, allowing
for high-accuracy predictions.
Unsupervised learning deals with data that has no prede-
fined labels. Instead, the model identifies patterns and rela-
tionships within the data through clustering, dimensionality
reduction, and association rule learning. Popular algorithms
include k-means clustering [34], hierarchical clustering [35],
and principal component analysis (PCA) [36]. This technique
is useful for anomaly detection, customer segmentation, and
workload clustering, where predefined categories do not ex-
ist, but patterns need to be discovered automatically.
RL is a technique in which an agent learns optimal be-
havior by interacting with an environment and receiving
rewards or penalties. It is particularly useful for decision-
making problems where actions must be taken sequentially
to maximize long-term rewards. Key RL algorithms include
Q-learning [37], deep Q-networks (DQN) [38], and policy
gradient methods [39]. This approach has been successfully
applied to robotics, game playing (e.g., AlphaGo), and system
optimization.
DL is a subset of ML that focuses on neural networks with
multiple layers (deep neural networks). It excels at process-
ing large and complex datasets, learning high-level feature
representations without manual intervention. DL techniques
include convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image pro-
cessing [40], recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequential
data [41], and transformers for natural language processing
(NLP) [42]. These methods have been widely applied in fields
such as computer vision, speech recognition, natural language
understanding, and system monitoring.

Abstract—In NAND ﬂash-based solid-state drives (SSDs), sys-
tem performance and quality of service tend to be degraded by
frequent conﬂicts between garbage collection (GC) I/Os and user
I/Os. To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive workload
burst-Aware Garbage Collection (AGC) mechanism to build high-
performance SSDs. AGC minimizes conﬂicts between user I/Os
and GC I/Os by jointly considering access patterns in workloads,
internal GC, and allocation strategies. The running time of a
workload is divided into multiple ﬁve-millisecond time windows.
AGC incorporates a burst I/O access pattern prediction mecha-
nism, which anticipates I/Os patterns in subsequent time windows
according to historical access patterns. Pattern predictions allow
AGC to proactively buffer valid pages during GC to prevent
interference with forthcoming user I/O requests. According to the
status of the underlying ﬂash memory, we implement a hybrid
allocation strategy to reduce GC-induced user writes blocking
while preserving read parallelism performance. AGC classiﬁes
data into four hotness levels (hot, warm, cool, and cold) according
to the update interval of the same request. Then, we design
a hotness-aware victim block selection policy that prioritizes
hot blocks to avert valid data migration during GC, thereby
reducing write ampliﬁcation in SSDs. We evaluate AGC through
extensive experiments driven by real-world traces. The ﬁndings
conﬁrm that compared with state-of-the-art schemes (Baseline,
CachedGC, FFT-GC, HIPA, and RDA), AGC reduces read and
write response time by up to 81.57% and 69.66%, respectively,
with average reductions of 54.34% and 39.21%. Furthermore,

hybrid SSDs. Then, based on the analysis, a differential TRIM

When free data superblocks run out, a victim data superblock with the most invalid pages is chosen for GC. A ﬂash page may be referenced by multiple LPNs due to address remapping. The FTL maintains a reference counting table (RC-table) to track the number of references for each ﬂash page. A ﬂash page is invalidated only when its reference count is zero. Considering most ﬂash pages have small refer- ence counts (e.g., smaller than ten [1]), four-bit counters are used by default. During the GC, valid data pages are moved to free ﬂash pages of a new data superblock. Meanwhile, new RMM entries are generated by updating the valid RMM entries (precisely, PPN ﬁelds) of migrated data pages and then written to the local log of the new data superblock. An RMM entry is identiﬁed as valid only when its P2L mapping is consis- tent with the latest L2P mapping. Afterward, the victim data superblock is erased to be free and its local log is invalidated.
The GC of RMM is conducted on both NVRAM segments and RMM superblocks. Instead of recording the validity status of every RMM entry, the FTL tracks the numbers of invalid RMM entries in the NVRAM segment groups and in the RMM page group for each data superblock. Speciﬁcally, a bitmap is maintained for LPNs and each entry contains two bits, called LR-bitmap. One bit indicates whether the current L2P mapping of an LPN is established by a remap or write operation. For a remapped LPN, the other bit records whether the relevant RMM entry is stored in the NVRAM segment group or the RMM page group. When an LPN previously remapped to a PPN is remapped again or written to a new PPN, the stale RMM entry becomes invalid and the number of invalid entries of the corresponding group increases by one.

RARO is implemented in FEMU [8], a QEMU-based

and SLC/TLC blocks appear only after mode conversions. To
evaluate the effectiveness of RARO, we compared it against

based mode conversion and migration scheme. Workloads

random reads. We evaluated the performance improvements of
RARO under different wear levels. Compared to the Baseline,
random read IOPS increased by 9.3 to 14.25 times. Compared
to Hotness, RARO achieved similar IOPS performance while
significantly reducing capacity loss.
The major contributions of this work are as follows:
• We analyze read retry behavior across flash modes and
identify its impact on read latency, motivating a retry-
aware mode management approach.
• We propose a migration policy based on both flash
reliability and data hotness to selectively switch storage
modes, reducing unnecessary mode conversions and pre-
serving storage capacity.
• We simulate the proposed RARO approach using work-
loads with various access skewness. Experimental results
show that RARO significantly improves read performance
with minimal capacity overhead.

Liu et al. [82] introduced MLCache, an ML-based cache
management system that enhances space efficiency in multi-
stream NVMe SSDs. MLCache uses an ANN to predict reuse
distance, allowing it to dynamically allocate cache space
based on predicted workload behavior. This improves cache
hit rates and reduces memory fragmentation, especially under
multi-tenant environments where multiple I/O streams com-
pete for limited cache space. Expanding on this work, the
same research group proposed a fairness-aware extension of
MLCache [83], which dynamically adjusts cache partitions
to prevent resource monopolization by high-intensity tasks.
By classifying workloads based on their I/O characteristics
and continuously reallocating cache based on demand and
priority, the system ensures equitable resource sharing and
maintains overall system efficiency in shared SSD environ-
ments.
Li et al. [84] proposed RLAlloc, a deep RL-based resource
allocation framework for multi-stream SSDs. RLAlloc uses
a Deep Q-Network (DQN) to adaptively manage both cache
and bandwidth resources in response to real-time workload
metrics. Unlike heuristic methods, RLAlloc learns optimal
allocation strategies that minimize performance bottlenecks
while satisfying QoS requirements, enabling efficient multi-
stream processing in dynamic environments.

Systems Using Multiple Bloom Filters
Dongchul Park and David H.C. Du
Department of Computer Science and Engineering

Email: {park, du}@cs.umn.edu
Abstract—Hot data identiﬁcation can be applied to a variety of
ﬁelds. Particularly in ﬂash memory, it has a critical impact on its
performance (due to a garbage collection) as well as its life span
(due to a wear leveling). Although the hot data identiﬁcation
is an issue of paramount importance in ﬂash memory, little
investigation has been made. Moreover, all existing schemes focus
almost exclusively on a frequency viewpoint. However, recency
also must be considered equally with the frequency for eﬀective
hot data identiﬁcation. In this paper, we propose a novel hot
data identiﬁcation scheme adopting multiple bloom ﬁlters to
eﬃciently capture ﬁner-grained recency as well as frequency.
In addition to this scheme, we propose a Window-based Direct
Address Counting (WDAC) algorithm to approximate an ideal
hot data identiﬁcation as our baseline. Unlike the existing baseline
algorithm that cannot appropriately capture recency information
due to its exponential batch decay, our WDAC algorithm, using
a sliding window concept, can capture very ﬁne-grained recency
information. Our experimental evaluation with diverse realistic
workloads including real SSD traces demonstrates that our
multiple bloom ﬁlter-based scheme outperforms the state-of-the-
art scheme. In particular, ours not only consumes 50% less
memory and requires less computational overhead up to 58%,
but also improves its performance up to 65%.
Index Terms—Hot Data Idenﬁciation, Hot and Cold Data,
Bloom Filter, Flash Memory, SSD, WDAC

IV. EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we first describe our experimental environ-
ment. Then, we present the results obtained using our devel-
opment board and compare the performance of our scheme to
the conventional one.
A. Experimental setup
In order to evaluate the performance of our scheme, we
conducted the evaluation on a PC with a 3.40GHz CPU and
8GB RAM. The system ran on Linux kernel version 4.5.4. We
compared our scheme to the baseline using EXT4 file system
for both ordered and data journaling modes.
We conducted experiments using synthetic and real-world
workloads. We used the FIO benchmark to generate synthetic
workloads and also used Filebench [23] and Sysbench [24] to
generate various real-world workloads.
Our experiments address the following questions:
 How effectively does our scheme manage journal writes
compared to the baseline?
 How much can our scheme reduce the latency of the
journal writes?
 How effective is our scheme in terms of performance?
 How effective is our scheme in terms of endurance?
B. Management of journal writes
In order to answer the first question, we compared the perfor-
mance by varying the amount of journal writes. We used 8KB
random write workloads generated by the FIO benchmark and
invoked fsync()

and GC lead to increased WA, which accelerates wear and
degrades performance. Recent research has applied ML tech-
niques to improve data classification, lifetime prediction, and
placement scheduling, thereby reducing WA and enhancing
endurance.
Sun et al. [58] proposed PHFTL, an SSD-embedded ML
framework that predicts data lifespan and separates short-
lived from long-lived data to improve placement efficiency.
Unlike host-side classification methods that impose addi-
tional overhead, PHFTL uses a lightweight on-device se-
quence model to classify data based on access frequency and
update behavior. A gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based page
classifier identifies short-lived data and ensures it is written to
distinct blocks, minimizing GC overhead. An adaptive label-
ing mechanism further refines classification by dynamically
adjusting thresholds for accuracy.
Lu et al. [59] developed a real-time classification approach
using K-means clustering and the classification and regres-
sion trees (CART) algorithm to group data based on update
frequency and longevity. The method includes an offline
phase to learn classification rules from historical write pat-
terns and an online phase for real-time block assignment.
By co-locating data with similar update characteristics, the
system reduces valid page migration during GC and mitigates
WA.
Chakraborttii et al. [60] introduced ML-DT, a temporal
convolutional network (TCN)-based model for LBA lifetime
prediction. In contrast to static classification schemes that
assign fixed update rates, ML-DT dynamically forecasts data
lifespan from historical access patterns. Grouping data with
similar expected death times prevents short-lived data from
triggering unnecessary movement of long-lived data during
GC. The model also supports workload generalization to
adapt across diverse usage patterns.

DUCTION
It is quite common for a single resource-rich contemporary
solid-state drive (SSD) to accommodate and execute multiple
workloads simultaneously. Such a shared SSD requires its
internal resources to be partitioned and allocated to co-running
workloads for preventing the competing workloads from in-
terfering with one another. While there exist various ways of
allocating the resources in an SSD, channel-based allocation
strategies are desirable from a performance standpoint, as they
can eliminate any potential interference between the workloads,
and thus, offer performance isolation to each workload [8].
Unfortunately, existing channel-based allocation strategies
assume a specific scenario in which the number of co-running
workloads is quite small, and in turn, each workload can obtain
as many channels as it wants. However, such situations may
not occur in some environments (e.g., university, company)
where many users in an organization share a fixed amount of
resources. Instead, in such environments where the collective
demand of workloads exceeds the available channel capacity,
device operators can face a new critical problem: “what is the
optimal channel allocation for a given set of co-running work-
loads?” In this paper, we refer to this problem as the “channel
allocation problem” and present a novel online solution for it.
The channel allocation problem is quite challenging due
to the following reasons. First, there is no accepted, unified
definition of “optimality”. In situations of channel scarcity, an

Suppose that it consumes about 40 cycles during one bloom ﬁlter check for a mapping entry, we can estimate that it cost 0.1 ms if the frequency of controller inside SSDs is 0.4 GHz. For extra I/O overhead, every one hundred mapping entry checks will need four more DTP reads on average because the false-positive rate of the bloom ﬁlter is about 0.056. If one DTP read consumes 25 μs, every 100 mapping entry will produce 100 μs latency. Based on the discussion above, the additional latency of processing overheads for every one hundred mapping entry is about 100 × 0.1 μs + 100 μs = 110 μs. In order to reduce these overheads and save the limited processing power of SSDs, BIT-DTPI is used to provide more efﬁcient search for mapping entries when the difference of max and min LPNs in one DTP is not larger than the given threshold. To measure how much BIT-DTPI reduces the processing overheads, we collect the number of BIT-DTPIs and BF-DTPIs for HCFTL equipped with both two types of DTPI after processing different work- loads. The results show that the proportions of BIT-DTPIs ([COUNTBIT-DTPIs]/[COUNTBIT-DTPIs + COUNTBF-DTPIs ]) are more than 20% under different workloads. That means BIT-DTPI can reduce the additional latency of processing overheads of 110 μs × 20% = 22 μs for every 100 mapping entry checks, compared to the scheme only equipped with the BF-DTPI approach.

We conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the efﬁ- ciency of HCFTL in terms of average CMT hit ratio, average system response time, and standard deviation of the system response time. Because GC and wear leveling are common schemes implemented in SSDs to improve the usage of storage space and lifetime, respectively, and they also impose impor- tant impact on the response time, we take the number of GC operations and chip-level wear leveling into consideration in our experiments.

A. RELATED WORK
At present, there are two types of hybrid SSDs: hard
partitioning hybrid SSDs and soft partitioning hybrid SSDs.
In the hard partitioning hybrid SSDs, there are at least two
types of flash memory. The hard partition is determined
by the underlying physical flash memory, so the size of
the different partition is fixed. The FTL algorithms for the
hard partitioning hybrid SSDs include: CFTL [16], Com-

Yao proposed HDFTL [19], an on-demand hybrid FTL that
adaptively migrates data between SLC and MLC regions
according to workload characteristics, aiming to reduce un-
necessary data movement while improving write performance

In this paper, a new Hotness-Aware Machine Learning
based SSD management, called HAML-SSD, is proposed to
reduce the overhead of GCs in SSDs. We have identiﬁed
that in addition to the update frequency, the average update
time interval, which is the average time interval between two
adjacent updates to the same data page, is also critical to deﬁne
the ”hotness” of a data page. Therefore, both parameters are
used for clustering data with I/O access patterns. Based on
those two factors, data are scheduled to different queues. The
clustering algorithm uses the K-Means algorithm to distinguish
which group/queue data should be allocated to. Meanwhile, a
new machine learning based hardware unit is designed to speed
up the training process in the SSD. The training execution time
with the machine learning hardware unit has the same order
of the latency of the SSD I/O operation which is much faster
than that of a general processor. In the experimental results,
the HAML-SSD is capable of signiﬁcantly reducing the overall
response time of different traces compared to previous works
while remaining a low hardware overhead.

Fig. 2: The key factors which render our channel allocation problem quite challenging.
• Different Performance Benefits: The magnitude of the
performance improvement that can be achieved as a result of
allocating extra channels varies significantly within each work-
load as well as across different workloads. Fig. 2b shows the
achieved throughput of three workloads under varying number
of allocated channels (when each workload is executed indi-
vidually). While an increase in the allocation generally leads
to an increase in the throughput of a workload, the throughput
improvement changes radically across the workloads. Even for
each individual workload, the increase in its throughput does
not exhibit any uniform patterns. Due to such irregular benefits
of workloads under varying allocations, finding an optimal
allocation requires either an offline profiling or a model-based
performance estimation (which may not be accurate).
To address this, we develop an online, real execution-based
approach, which does not require any profiling or model-
based strategy. Specifically, inspired by the self-adapting nature
of reinforcement learning (RL), AutoAlloc evaluates each
allocation by executing the target workloads on it at runtime,
and identifies an optimal allocation in a gradual fashion based
on the cumulative evaluation results.
• Huge Search Space: The number of possible channel allo-
cations increases significantly, as the number of the available
channels in the target device and/or the competing workloads
increases. Fig. 2c shows the number of possible channel al-
locations for a few problem scenarios. Even in a tiny-scale
scenario where 4 workloads share 32 channels, there exist up
to a thousand of different allocations, which may require an
extensive experimental effort to evaluate candidate allocations.
